title: A mind that rests on nothing (section 10)
word: A mind that rests on nothing
hook: a mind should arise that rests on nothing: the line said to have woken Huineng

segments.voice: Yesterday, no I have attained: Subhuti dwells in peace without the thought that he has. Your line: without I did. Did a good deed go by without a signature? Day one thousand one hundred twenty-seven.

A young man is selling firewood in a market town in southern China. He's poor, and the old account says he can't read. He delivers a load to a shop, and on the way out he hears a man reciting something. The words stop him where he stands. He asks what the man is reciting. The Diamond Sutra, comes the answer. That's how the Platform Sutra, the book of this young man's life and teaching, tells it. His name is Huineng, and Chan and Zen remember him as a great ancestor. Later in the same account, one line of that sutra opens him all the way. It's today's.
screen: `A FIREWOOD SELLER.` → `A SUTRA HEARD IN PASSING.` → `HUINENG STOPS.`

segments.voice: First, a look back. The Buddha asks Subhuti: long ago, when the Tathagata was with the Buddha Dipankara, did he receive any teaching? No, Subhuti says. Nothing was received. Second, adorning. Does a bodhisattva adorn the Buddha-lands, make the worlds beautiful? No, Subhuti says, because adorning is not adorning; that's why it's called adorning. It's the rhythm of the earlier sections. Third, the line. Therefore, the Buddha says, a bodhisattva should give rise to a pure mind like this: a mind that doesn't rest on sights, doesn't rest on sounds, smells, tastes, touches or thoughts. A mind should arise that rests on nothing. Notice it doesn't say no mind should arise. The mind arises. It sees, it hears, it works. It just doesn't set up camp. A hand that catches a ball and lets it go is still a hand. Tradition says that later, when Huineng's teacher explained the sutra to him, it was at this line that he woke up completely. Fourth, a look back down the week. Giving without resting on anything. Not seen by marks. Even the raft. Nothing fixed. Four lines, passed on. No I have attained. Each of those days was a place where the mind could have settled down and made a home: the gift, the statue, the teaching, the prize, the credit. Each time, the sutra let it lift off again. Today's line names what was happening all week. It's the same mind, just not resting.
screen: `NOTHING RECEIVED FROM DIPANKARA.` · `ADORNING THAT ISN'T ADORNING.` · `A MIND THAT RESTS ON NOTHING.` · `A WEEK OF NOT SETTLING.` · then, large: `RESTING ON NOTHING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: notice one moment without clinging. Settle, and breathe. Let sounds come: a car, a fridge, your own breathing. Notice the mind land on one. That's a truck. That's too loud. Then let it lift, the way a bird lifts off a wire. Another sound comes; the mind lands; it lifts. You don't have to stop it landing. Just catch one moment of lifting, and stay in the open space after it, for as long as it lasts. When a thought sets up camp, notice, and let it go. The bell holds the time.
A mind that rests on nothing. A mind that arises without resting on sights, sounds or thoughts: the line tradition says woke Huineng. Today's word.
screen: `A MIND THAT RESTS ON NOTHING — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: resting on nothing. Today, when a worry lands and starts unpacking, notice it, and let it lift once, like a bird off a wire. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-seven.

howItsDone: In Chan and Zen this line is studied closely and often recited, and the story of Huineng hearing the Diamond Sutra is told in the Platform Sutra, a text read in those schools.

fork.setup: you're Huineng, selling firewood. a line from a stranger's recitation stops you in your tracks. what do you do?
options: finish the delivery and forget it.
ask what the text is, and where it's taught.
wait for him to recite it again tomorrow.
fork.reveal: he asks. the Platform Sutra says he learns it's the Diamond Sutra and hears of a teacher who teaches it, and he sets out to find him.

original.note: Sanskrit: not resting, not set down; the sutra's word for a mind that settles on nothing.

trapdoor: what you thought: an empty mind, with nothing in it.
what it means: a mind that arises and works, seeing and hearing, without setting up camp on any of it.
what a scholar hears: apratishthita, unsupported; the Platform Sutra ties the awakening of Huineng, honored in Chan and Zen, to this line.

notes: Section numbering follows the common 32-section division of Kumarajiva's Chinese text. The section's closing image (a body like Mount Sumeru) is left out for length.

The Huineng story is given as the Platform Sutra's account and 'tradition says'; versions of the Platform Sutra differ on details (e.g. whether he awakened on first hearing, or fully on Hongren's later explanation of this line). Check the wording against the version the path uses.
'Can't read' follows the Platform Sutra's account of Huineng as unlettered; confirm.
Hook's 'southern China' follows the Platform Sutra's setting; confirm wording.
Original: apratishthita (Sanskrit text has apratishthitam cittam utpadayitavyam); confirm spelling.

Editor pass: the hook said one line stopped Huineng in the market and that this was today's line; in the Platform Sutra he is moved by the recitation in general and awakens fully at this line later, when Hongren explains the sutra. The hook now says that. The reciter was a man leaving the shop, not necessarily the customer, so 'a customer' became 'a man' (hook and myth). Cut 'You know this rhythm by now' (telling the listener what they know).
